title: First record session, as Jabbo Smith's replacement
summary: He was told to stand in on the James P. Johnson record for the missing Jabbo Smith, and was introduced to the studio as Jabbo.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: And that was it, I think, wasn't it? Well, that's good. So there's the personnel on that. And then, I wanted to ask you about that record session that you made in 1928, where Jabbo disappeared. Jabbo Smith wasn't to be found. And somebody came and got you and got you to play on the James P. Johnson record, in Jabbo's place.

Yeah. They came by and said, 'Now, listen, Cootie, now you've got to take Jabbo's place, because we can't find him.' Me and Jabbo was two good buddies. And then, 'You are Jabbo. When you get down to the recording studio, we're going to call you Jabbo.'
(Laughter)
'Now, your name is Jabbo Smith.' I said, 'Okay, let's go.' So all during the record session, they
Jabbo was calling me Jabble.
(Laughter)
Who, James P. was?
Yeah.
Isn't that funny?
(Laughter)
That was your first record session, too.
Yeah. That was my first record session.
Funny, isn't it?
That's right.
So was there -- of course, you weren't nervous, because like you said, you never did get nervous.
No. I never did get nervous.
But did they just tell you how to stand to the microphone and all that, huh?
No. I don't know if that was my first record. I did a session with Fletcher.
Oh, you did. Of course you did.
They didn't let me do no solo.
Didn't they?
No.
No kidding. Which -- can you remember which session that was?
No, I don't remember.
So there's nothing that -- with Fletcher Henderson, there's not a single record with you blowing any solo on that?
No. No.

Isn't that funny. I didn't realize that. Oh, well, at least so you knew the ropes anyway, then it wasn't your first session. Well, good. So -- and then I guess that deluded a lot of people into thinking that was Jabbo on that, huh?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
People like Hugues Panassie in France. I mean, they must have been real surprised, because they could tell. You know, if people like that had a good ear, they could tell who they were listening to.
I don't think so. Not at that period of time.
Really?
No.
What do you mean?
Nobody knew. Because nobody knew me during that period.
Oh, of course. That's right. So they wouldn't recognize you.
No.
